lesson.title: Meet self: How an Object Talks About Itself
lesson.summary: The self parameter is how a method reaches back into the specific object it was called on, letting one block of code work correctly for every instance of a class.
lesson.body:
You already know how to write a class definition, a blueprint that describes what kind of data and behavior a group of objects will share. But there's a puzzle hiding inside that blueprint. If a class only defines its methods once, and you can create a hundred different objects from that class, how does a method called on object number 47 know to work with object number 47's data instead of someone else's? The answer is a parameter named self, and understanding it is the single most important step in learning to write real classes.

When you define a method inside a class, its first parameter is, by strong convention, named self. You never pass a value for self yourself. Instead, Python fills it in automatically with whatever object sits to the left of the dot when the method is called. Write fido.bark() and Python quietly translates that into Dog.bark(fido), handing the method a direct reference to fido as its first argument. Inside the method, self.name means "the name attribute that belongs to whichever object called me," which is exactly the flexibility a shared blueprint needs.

Here's a small class without an __init__ method yet (you'll meet that in the next chapter) to keep the focus purely on self:

```python
class Dog:
    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

fido = Dog()
fido.name = "Fido"
print(fido.bark())
# Output: Fido says Woof!

# These two calls do exactly the same thing:
print(Dog.bark(fido))
# Output: Fido says Woof!
```

Trace through it carefully. fido = Dog() creates a new, essentially empty object. The line fido.name = "Fido" attaches an attribute called name directly onto that object. Then fido.bark() runs the bark method with self bound to fido, so self.name resolves to "Fido" and the method returns the string "Fido says Woof!". The second call, Dog.bark(fido), proves there's no magic involved: it calls the exact same function, just with fido supplied by hand instead of automatically through the dot. That equivalence is the whole trick behind self, it is simply the object before the dot, made available inside the method.

self is not a reserved keyword in Python. You could technically name that first parameter anything you like, and the code would still run. But every Python programmer, every tutorial, and every piece of professional code uses self, so breaking that convention only makes your code harder for others (and future you) to read. Get comfortable writing self as the first parameter of every method you define inside a class, because from here forward, it's how every method reaches into the specific object it's working on.
